html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Name the control plane and node components and what each does
  • Explain declarative configuration, desired state and reconciliation
  • Read the API's groups, versions and kinds and the parts of a manifest
  • Use labels, selectors, annotations, namespaces and owner references
  • Recognize custom resources, operators and the ways to get a cluster

2Control plane, nodes, components, add-ons, the path of a request, what the exam asks

Running case

Harbor Books Gets a Cluster

  • The platform engineer is handed a new cluster and has to learn what is inside it
  • The team will describe the shop in files and let Kubernetes make it so
  • People will need to find all the storefront Pods, and to keep staging apart from production
  • In this module you map the parts of the cluster and the objects the team will use

A Cluster: Control Plane and Nodes

  • A cluster is a control plane plus worker nodes
  • The control plane makes global decisions and manages the nodes and the Pods
  • Nodes are the worker machines that run the Pods; a node can be a virtual or a physical machine
  • In production the control plane usually runs across several machines

Exam tip

The control plane decides; the nodes run the Pods.

Control Plane Components

Component What it does
kube-apiserver serves the Kubernetes API; the front end of the control plane
etcd keeps all cluster data in a consistent, highly available key-value store
kube-scheduler picks a node for each new Pod that has none
kube-controller-manager runs the controllers that keep the cluster at its desired state
cloud-controller-manager links the cluster to a cloud provider's API; a local or on-premises cluster has none
  • etcd holds all cluster data, so it needs a backup plan
Exam tip

API server is the front door, etcd is the memory, the scheduler places Pods and the controller manager runs the loops.

Node Components and Add-ons

  • The kubelet is an agent on each node that makes sure the containers of its Pods are running
  • kube-proxy is a network proxy on each node that implements part of the Service idea; it is optional, because some network plugins do the job themselves
  • The container runtime runs the containers (module 1)
  • Add-ons extend the cluster; every cluster should have cluster DNS

Exam tip

kubelet and kube-proxy run on every node; the scheduler and API server do not.

Following a Request: From kubectl to a Running Pod

  • You send a request with kubectl to the API server
  • The object is stored in etcd
  • The scheduler notices a Pod with no node and picks a node
  • The kubelet on that node starts the containers and reports status
  • Components talk to each other through the API server

Exam tip

When a question asks who stores, who places and who runs, the answers are etcd, the scheduler and the kubelet.

What the Exam Asks: Architecture

  • Control plane or node: API server, etcd, scheduler and controller manager decide; kubelet and kube-proxy run on every node
  • Declarative or imperative: declarative states the result and uses apply
  • spec or status: you write the spec; Kubernetes writes the status
  • Label or annotation: labels select; annotations only inform
  • Group or version: apps/v1 is group and version; the core group is plain v1
  • CRD or operator: a CRD adds a kind; an operator adds a controller for it
Exam tip

For a "which component" question, picture the request path: API server, etcd, scheduler, kubelet.

3Declarative versus imperative, controllers and the reconciliation loop

Declarative Versus Imperative

Technique Works on Example
Imperative commands live objects kubectl create deployment storefront --image=...
Imperative object configuration individual files kubectl create -f storefront.yaml
Declarative object configuration directories of files kubectl apply -f ./manifests
  • Declarative means you state the desired result in files; Kubernetes works out the steps
  • kubectl apply is the recommended way to manage applications in production
Exam tip

Declarative describes the end state; imperative gives the steps.

Controllers and the Reconciliation Loop

  • A controller is a control loop that watches the cluster's state through the API server
  • It acts to narrow the gap between the current state and the desired state
  • A thermostat is the classic example: it compares the room to the setting and acts
  • kube-controller-manager runs many controllers in one process

Exam tip

Self-healing in Kubernetes is just controllers reconciling.

4API groups, versions and kinds, manifests, the common kinds, kubectl, kubeconfig

The API: Groups, Versions and Kinds

Group Path apiVersion Kinds, for example
Core /api/v1 v1 Pod, Service, ConfigMap, Namespace
Named /apis/GROUP/VERSION apps/v1, batch/v1 Deployment, StatefulSet, Job, CronJob
  • alpha (for example v1alpha1): off by default; support can be dropped at any time
  • beta (for example v1beta1): new built-in beta versions are also off by default
  • stable (v1, v2): named vX with an integer
Exam tip

apiVersion is group and version; the core group is written as plain v1.

Anatomy of a Manifest

  • apiVersion: which version of the API you use; kind: what kind of object
  • metadata: identifying data, such as a name, a UID (unique ID) and an optional namespace
  • spec: the desired state, which you write
  • status: the current state, which Kubernetes writes and keeps updated
  • An object is a record of intent: once created, Kubernetes works to keep it so

A minimal Pod manifest

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: storefront
  namespace: shop
  labels:
    app: storefront
spec:
  containers:
  - name: storefront
    image: harborbooks/storefront:1.4
Exam tip

You write the spec; Kubernetes writes the status.

Kinds You Will Meet

Kind What it is Module
Pod one or more containers run together Module 3
Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob controllers that run Pods Module 3
ConfigMap, Secret configuration and sensitive settings Module 4
Service, Ingress stable network access to Pods Module 6
PersistentVolumeClaim a request for storage Module 7
Namespace, Node a scope for names; a worker machine Module 2
Exam tip

Learn the kind names now; the next modules explain each one.

kubectl: the Command Line

  • kubectl talks to the cluster's control plane through the API; you can create, inspect, update and delete objects
  • Syntax: kubectl [command] [TYPE] [NAME] [flags]
  • Resource types are case-insensitive; names are case-sensitive
  • kubectl explain documents a resource; kubectl api-resources lists the kinds

Everyday kubectl commands

kubectl get pods -n shop
kubectl describe pod storefront -n shop
kubectl apply -f storefront.yaml
kubectl delete pod storefront -n shop
kubectl explain pods
kubectl api-resources
Exam tip

get lists, describe explains, apply declares, delete removes.

kubeconfig: Clusters, Users and Contexts

  • A kubeconfig file lists clusters, users and contexts
  • A context ties a cluster, a user and a namespace together; current-context says which one is active
  • By default kubectl reads the config file in the .kube folder of your home directory; KUBECONFIG or --kubeconfig points elsewhere
  • kubectl config get-contexts lists contexts and kubectl config use-context switches
  • Use kubeconfig files only from trusted sources

A small kubeconfig

apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:
- name: production
  cluster: {server: "https://k8s.harborbooks.example"}
users:
- name: platform-engineer
contexts:
- name: prod-shop
  context: {cluster: production, user: platform-engineer, namespace: shop}
current-context: prod-shop
Exam tip

The context decides which cluster, user and namespace the next command uses.

5Labels, selectors, annotations, namespaces, owner references

Labels, Selectors and Annotations

  • Labels are key/value pairs on objects: identifying attributes that are meaningful to users
  • A selector filters objects by their labels; selecting by label is the main way Kubernetes groups objects
  • Services and controllers use selectors to find their Pods
  • Annotations hold non-identifying metadata for tools and people; they can be large and unstructured

Exam tip

Labels select; annotations do not.

Namespaces and Owner References

  • Namespaces isolate groups of resources within one cluster; a name must be unique inside one namespace, and another namespace may reuse it
  • Namespaces cannot be nested, and each object is in one namespace
  • Four start with every cluster: default, kube-node-lease, kube-public and kube-system
  • Owner references record which objects depend on which, so the control plane cleans up the right ones
  • Ownership is not the same as labels and selectors

Exam tip

A namespace scopes names and policies; ownership drives clean-up.

6Custom resources, operators, where clusters come from

Custom Resources, Controllers and Operators

  • A CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) adds a new kind to the API, without building a custom API server
  • Custom resources are used with kubectl just like built-in objects
  • A custom controller keeps them at their desired state
  • The operator pattern links a controller to custom resources to automate what a human operator would do

Exam tip

A CRD adds a kind; an operator adds the controller that acts on it.

Where Clusters Come From Beyond the curriculum

Option What it is
Managed service you choose a service instead of running the cluster yourself
kubeadm a tool that installs Kubernetes and sets up a secure cluster
kind local clusters that use Docker containers as nodes
minikube a local cluster for macOS, Linux and Windows
k3s lightweight, fully conformant Kubernetes in a single binary
  • Self-managed means you run the control plane and the nodes yourself
Exam tip

kubeadm builds clusters; kind and minikube are for learning; k3s is the lightweight one.

7Exam Q&A

7.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1Where does Kubernetes keep all of its cluster data?

  • AIn the kubelet that runs on each worker node of the cluster
  • BIn memory inside the kube-scheduler, which rebuilds it after a restart
  • CIn etcd, a consistent and highly available key-value store
  • DIn the image cache of the container runtime on every node
Show the answer

Answer: C. etcd is the backing store for all cluster data, which is why it needs a backup plan. The kubelet runs Pods, the scheduler picks nodes, and the runtime's image cache holds images, not cluster state.

S2A Harbor Books Pod has been created but is not yet assigned to any node. Which component picks a node for it?

  • AThe kube-scheduler, which selects a node for each new Pod without one
  • BThe kubelet, which assigns Pods to the nodes that have free memory
  • CThe kube-proxy, which decides where Pods run according to Service rules
  • DThe etcd store, which places each new object on the least busy node
Show the answer

Answer: A. The kube-scheduler watches for new Pods with no node and selects one. The kubelet runs the Pods that are assigned to its node, kube-proxy maintains network rules, and etcd only stores data.

S3What does the kubelet do?

  • AIt chooses a node for every Pod that has not yet been assigned to one
  • BIt runs the controller loops that keep the cluster at its desired state
  • CIt maintains the network rules that implement part of the Service idea
  • DIt makes sure the containers described in its node's Pods are running
Show the answer

Answer: D. The kubelet is the agent on each node that makes sure the containers of its Pods are running. Choosing nodes is the scheduler's job, the controller loops belong to the controller manager, and network rules belong to kube-proxy.

S4The Harbor Books team keeps its storefront manifests in a directory and wants Kubernetes to create or update whatever differs. Which command follows the declarative approach?

  • Akubectl create deployment storefront --image=harborbooks/storefront:1.4
  • Bkubectl apply -f ./manifests
  • Ckubectl scale deployment storefront --replicas=3
  • Dkubectl delete -f ./manifests
Show the answer

Answer: B. Declarative configuration states the desired result in files, and kubectl apply makes the cluster match them. Creating a Deployment from flags and scaling it are imperative commands, and deleting removes objects.

S5A controller finds fewer running Pods than the desired state asks for. What does it do?

  • AIt creates or requests the changes that move the current state toward the desired state
  • BIt waits for an administrator to approve the change before it acts
  • CIt rewrites the spec so that it matches the Pods that are running now
  • DIt stops watching the object until the next Kubernetes release arrives
Show the answer

Answer: A. A controller is a control loop: it compares the current state with the desired state and acts to close the gap. It does not wait for approval, it does not edit the spec you wrote, and it keeps watching.

S6Which apiVersion belongs in a Deployment manifest?

  • Av1, the version of the core group
  • Bbatch/v1, the group of Jobs
  • Capps/v1, the group of workload controllers
  • Dapps/v1alpha1, an early version of the same group
Show the answer

Answer: C. Deployments are in the apps group, version v1, written apps/v1. The core group is written as plain v1 and holds kinds such as Pod and Service, batch/v1 holds Jobs and CronJobs, and an alpha version is off by default.

S7Which statement about API versions is correct?

  • AAlpha versions are switched on by default and supported for many releases
  • BBeta versions such as v1beta1 are the only ones that are safe for production
  • CA stable version name contains the word stable, as in stable1
  • DA stable version is named vX with an integer X, such as v1
Show the answer

Answer: D. Stable versions are named vX where X is an integer. Alpha versions are off by default and may be dropped at any time, new built-in beta versions are also off by default, and no version name contains the word stable.

S8A Service must find all the storefront Pods. Which feature does it use?

  • AAnnotations, which carry non-identifying information about each Pod
  • BA label selector, which picks the Pods that carry matching labels
  • COwner references, which record that a Deployment owns its Pods
  • DA namespace, which groups every Pod that the cluster has ever run
Show the answer

Answer: B. Selecting by label is how Services and controllers find their Pods: they pick the Pods whose labels match. Annotations are not used to select, owner references drive clean-up, and a namespace scopes names rather than choosing Pods.

S9Two teams want to use the same object name in one cluster without a clash. What provides the separation?

  • AA label, which makes the name unique across the whole cluster
  • BAn annotation, which reserves the name for one of the two teams
  • CA namespace, which scopes names so that each namespace can reuse them
  • DA UID, which Kubernetes then uses in place of the object's name
Show the answer

Answer: C. A name must be unique inside one namespace, and another namespace may reuse it, so two teams can each use their own. Labels and annotations do not scope names, and the UID is generated by Kubernetes in addition to the name.

S10What does a CustomResourceDefinition do?

  • AIt adds a new kind of object to the API without a custom API server
  • BIt starts a controller that restarts Pods when their containers fail
  • CIt tells the scheduler which nodes a Pod is allowed to run on
  • DIt stores a backup copy of all the data held in the cluster
Show the answer

Answer: A. A CRD defines a new kind that is served by the existing API server, and its objects are used with kubectl like built-in ones. Restarting containers is the kubelet's job, node choice is scheduling, and backups are a separate task.

S11The Harbor Books team installs software that adds a Database kind to the API, plus a controller that creates, backs up and repairs databases from those objects. What is this pattern called?

  • AA kube-proxy mode, which routes traffic to the databases
  • BA ReplicaSet strategy, which keeps a set number of Pods
  • CA cloud-controller-manager, which links the cluster to a cloud
  • DAn operator, which links a controller to custom resources
Show the answer

Answer: D. An operator is a controller linked to custom resources that automates what a human operator would do. kube-proxy handles networking, a ReplicaSet keeps a number of Pods running, and the cloud-controller-manager talks to a cloud provider.

8Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Cluster a control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager) and nodes (kubelet, kube-proxy, runtime)
Declarative state the desired result; controllers reconcile the current state toward it
API and manifests group and version, kind, metadata, spec, status; use kubectl and a kubeconfig
Organizing objects labels select, annotations inform, namespaces scope names, owner references drive clean-up
Extending CRDs add kinds, operators add controllers
